papers.title: Decline and extirpation of birds in a tropical Asian grassland ecosystem over the past century
papers.abstract: Grasslands are facing unprecedented habitat loss due to settler-driven agriculture during colonial expansion, conversion to tree plantations, misclassification as wastelands, absorption into megadevelopment projects, and insufficient response to climate change. Globally, grassland birds have faced the steepest declines, with many formerly common species facing rapid decline, losing much of their original ranges. In South Asia, our knowledge of how these land-use changes in grasslands have affected birds remain scant. Natural history collections and archives are vital resources to identify historical baselines for conducting a resurvey and identifying trends in long-term biodiversity response. Yet such historical data remain insufficient in tropical regions. In this study, by compiling an unprecedented dataset of ornithological surveys from the 1900s using a diverse set of historical data, we conducted a 3-year resurvey in an Eastern Himalayan grassland first surveyed by British Ornithologist Herbert Stevens. We surveyed nine historical localities. Using a recently developed Bayesian method to calibrate modern surveys with historical museum data, we found a 70.5% decline in grassland specialist birds. We also report the local extirpation of four endemic species of grassland birds. Open habitat raptors showed a 74.9% decline, while generalist species showed an increase of 23.5% and wetland birds showed a marginal increase of 2.64%. By quantifying functional distinctiveness, a measure of morphological diversity, we find that loss of grassland species does not impact morphological and functional diversity in modern assemblage. We also find that most resurvey localities have a high number of invasive species that have completely altered these communities. Grassland specialist birds of South Asia are highly range-restricted and have specific habitat requirements; the lack of intact tall grass communities in concert with site-level disturbance pressures from grazing, conversion and fire have likely contributed to their local extirpation. Our study serves as one of the first efforts to resurvey wet grasslands of South Asia and document local-level extirpation. We also highlight the importance of museum-based research to document long-term changes for urgent conservation attention.

papers.title: Effects of drying and milling treatments on estimates of foliar functional traits with VSWIR spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Spectroscopy of dried, ground foliage is a cost-efficient measurement to estimate leaf biochemical traits in agricultural and ecological research. Drying removes water that obscures biochemical absorption features, and milling homogenizes samples, yet how drying and milling methods affect spectra and trait predictions is understudied. We compared two drying methods (oven-drying; flash-freezing then freeze-drying) and three milling methods (coarse and fine rotary milling; ball milling) using 61 individuals of 11 broadleaf and needle- or scale-leaved woody species. Mean reflectance differences between milling treatments ranged 1.7-4.6% across the full spectrum and were largest between fine and coarse rotary milling. Freeze-dried samples had on average 7.2% higher reflectance than oven-dried samples, with larger differences in broadleaf species. Bayesian ANOVAs of spectrally predicted nitrogen and calcium demonstrated that drying had the largest effect, and that fine and ball milling also shifted predictions relative to coarse milling, but all treatment effects were smaller than interspecific variation. Although the partial least squares regression models were trained on oven-dried material, freeze-dried and more finely milled samples had lower prediction error (NRMSE) than oven-dried samples. Our finding emphasize that sample processing methods should be carefully documented for studies measuring traits from foliar spectroscopy.

papers.title: Cryptic viruses shape trophic networks after biological invasions
papers.abstract: Biological invasions restructure ecological communities by bringing previously isolated organisms into contact, but the viral flow within the trophic network and its consequences have not been established. Here, we show viral exchange following the introduction of a parasitoid wasp released for classical biological control in citrus. Within a few years, viruses spread bidirectionally between native and exotic host-parasitoid trophic chains and reached a generalist hyperparasitoid at the fourth trophic level. Cohabitation and multiparasitism, two ubiquitous interactions between the two trophic chains, were sufficient for viruses to be transferred between species and maintained transgenerationally. A virus acquired by the introduced parasitoid increased its offspring production by 30%. Our results identify cryptic viruses as an overlooked dimension of biological invasions, reshaping trophic networks and the outcome of the species we deliberately introduce.

papers.title: Will they survive? The critical status of Asiatic cheetahs in Iran
papers.abstract: The Asiatic cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus venaticus), once widespread, now survives only in Iran, with its population nearing extinction. In this study, we synthesised 13 years (2012 to 2024) of monitoring data to assess demographic and spatial patterns of this critically endangered subspecies in Iran. Using extensive camera trap surveys across eight reserves, supplemented by published records of cheetah occurrences on social media, we identified 24 adult cheetahs in the Northern and Southern Landscapes. No reproduction or new individuals have been recorded in the Southern Landscape for over a decade, while the Northern Landscape supports the remaining population, likely fewer than 30 adult individuals. From 2012 to 2024, at least 38 cubs were born from eight females in the Northern Landscape, with 74.1% surviving their first year. The absence of any newly detected adults throughout the 13-year study period suggests that long-term individual-based monitoring has likely captured the entire known adult population. Asiatic cheetahs show high mobility, often crossing unprotected communal lands and a major highway, increasing mortality risks. Camera traps enabled us to effectively identify individuals but are limited for tracking fine-scale movements, underscoring the need for satellite telemetry. Roadside fencing, wildlife underpasses, habitat protection, community-based land management, and stronger anti-trafficking measures are critical to enhance survival. Genetic risks, including low population size and inbreeding, further threaten viability. These findings inform conservation strategies for endangered carnivores in arid ecosystems. Keywords: arid environment, camera trap, illegal wildlife trade, population viability, small population

papers.title: Community responses outweigh species-level plasticity in shaping future marine forests
papers.abstract: Anthropogenic ocean warming (OW) and acidification (OA) are progressively reshaping marine ecosystems, yet ecosystem-level evidence remains limited. Marine forests are foundational ecosystems that support highly productive and diverse communities. Understanding how macroalgal communities will assemble, perform and persist in future ocean conditions requires integrated evidence capturing concurrent shifts in primary productivity, species interactions, and associated macroalgal community responses. Here, we provide a multi-level approach combining laboratory experiments with field surveys to assess how Mediterranean marine macroalgal forests will respond to future warming and acidification. We used local populations from natural CO2; vents in Panarea (Aeolian Islands, Italy) and present-day pH conditions of the emblematic forest-forming species Ericaria balearica to quantify multi-level responses to future climate drivers. Specifically, we crossed temperature (present day, T+2 C, T+4 C), pH (present day pHT ~ 7.9, low pHT ~7.6), and origin population (ambient vs CO2 vents) in laboratory experiments, where we measured changes in Ericaria biomass and metabolism, as well as herbivory by the sea urchin Paracentrotus lividus. We also assessed in situ community structure by quantifying species-specific percent cover and biomass along a pH gradient. In natural CO2 vents, E. balearica biomass was greater than at ambient sites, and associated macroalgal community composition differed between pH zones. In the laboratory, across the simulated spring-summer warming period, E. balerarica biomass declined similarly in all treatments with no important effect of pH; a marginal signal suggested that vent-origin individuals retained more biomass only under present-day temperature. Sea urchin consumption was reduced under low pH and showed a weaker response to temperature. Overall, we found no clear direct impact of OWxOA on E. balearica performance but significant influence of OA on herbivory and the associated macroalgal community, indicating that ecological processes outweigh the effects at the individual or population level.

papers.title: Resource enrichment and utilization underlie widely observed production and biomass scaling relationships
papers.abstract: Broadly observed trophic scaling patterns relate the biomass of predators to the biomass of prey, and biomass to productivity. The consistency with which these patterns are observed suggests the existence of governing principles that apply across ecosystems. We present a model for the trophic interaction between phytoplankton and zooplankton that produces the scaling patterns as an emergent property of resource enrichment without invoking the influence of phenotypic or genotypic diversity on system structure. Using formulations with broad empirical support, the model incorporates processes that are common to all ecosystems: resource enrichment, feeding, growth, maintenance, and mortality. Thus, our interpretation of widely observed scaling relationships provides constraints for models that quantify the coupling between ecosystem structure and elemental cycles across terrestrial and aquatic environments.

papers.title: Microeukaryotic indicators of freshwater ecosystem condition from a national river monitoring network
papers.abstract: Microeukaryotes are a diverse and functionally important component of river biofilms, including primary producers, consumers, decomposers, and parasites and symbionts. However, their diversity is likely underestimated, and their composition, environmental drivers, and seasonal dynamics have rarely been studied at large spatial scales. Microbiological monitoring of freshwater ecosystems has historically focused almost entirely on diatoms, so the potential of the wider microbial community as indicators of river condition is unknown. Here, we used 18S rRNA gene metabarcoding of more than 1,600 biofilm samples from 700 sites across England's River Surveillance Network. We show that communities were dominated by diatoms, chlorophytes, ciliates, and fungi, and shifted from phototroph-dominated biofilms in spring towards more diverse, heterotroph-rich biofilms in autumn. Community turnover was driven by water chemistry rather than geographic distance, with alkalinity, DO, temperature, and nitrate-N among the strongest drivers of composition. Co-occurrence networks resolved assemblages of taxa with shared environmental responses, and threshold indicator taxa analysis identified ASV-level indicators of water chemistry gradients. Community change points along these gradients closely matched those reported for bacteria from the same biofilms, and several taxa declined at lower concentrations than the community as a whole, offering potential early warning of change. These findings show that the microeukaryotic community tracks water chemistry consistently across a national river network and can provide a taxonomically broad set of sensitive and interpretable indicators of river condition that complement diatom-based monitoring and emerging bacterial approaches.

papers.title: A unifying framework for structured population dynamics in modern coexistence theory
papers.abstract: Variation within populations is ubiquitous in nature, yet many models and frameworks in community ecology assume that all individuals within a population interact with the community identically. Modern coexistence theory is no exception; however, several subfields of ecology have independently been integrating coexistence theory, each asking the same underlying question: how do structured population dynamics shape coexistence outcomes? Here, I propose a unifying framework for integrating population variation into modern coexistence theory that is applicable across all fields of ecology. The application of this framework is presented in three case studies: niche overlap and fitness differences between influenza substrains, mutual invasibility between competing perennial plants, and fluctuation-dependent invasion outcomes in apparently competing prey with a foraging-predation risk tradeoff. Together, these examples illustrate the framework's broad applicability, power to resolve the interaction between population and community level processes, and its potential to reveal novel ecological phenomena.

papers.title: Synergistic mechanistic and deep learning approaches for modeling insect thermal responses and geographic distributions
papers.abstract: Aim The Hutchinsonian shortfall, the lack of knowledge about species' abiotic tolerance, limits our understanding of species responses to environmental change and consequently also the outlining of their distribution in space and time. Such environmental tolerance is commonly inferred with two distinct approaches: i) trait performance studies, which use lab experiments to model species' functional responses, often overlooking real-world complexity, and ii) species distribution models, which infer environmental suitability from occurrence data, but offer limited causal insights. In this paper, we argue that these two strategies bring complementary information that can be integrated to estimate species-environment relationships more robustly and accurately map species distributions. Location Global scale Time period 2000-2019 Major taxa studied Given their exceptional diversity and climatic sensitivity, insects provide a powerful system for studying these responses. We selected key insect species representing i) disease vectors: the yellow fever (Aedes aegypti) and Asian tiger (Aedes albopictus) mosquitoes; ii) agricultural pests: the cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) and the fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda); and iii) biocontrol agents: the green lacewing (Chrysoperla carnea) and the 14-spotted ladybug (Propylea quatuordecimpunctata). Methods We compared predicted insect thermal suitability and distributions derived from two complementary methodological approaches: mechanistic models based on experimentally derived thermal responses of ecological rates, and deep learning-based species distribution models based on occurrence data. We further tested hybrid frameworks integrating mechanistic and correlational information through model ensembling, mechanistic regularization, and mechanistically informed deep learning. We assessed the efficacy of these methods under increasing data scarcity by progressively removing up to 80% of species occurrence records using three strategies: removal from the warmest or coldest parts of species' thermal ranges, removal from the least-sampled locations based on geographic sampling bias, and random removal as a baseline. Results Our findings highlight that occurrence-derived thermal suitability closely reproduces the observed distributions of insects. Compared to the mechanistic estimates, these thermal response curves are consistently shifted towards lower temperatures, potentially reflecting niche underfilling. However, when challenged with progressive data removal, correlative methods fail to extrapolate reliably in data-deficient regimes, where mechanistic knowledge becomes increasingly more crucial. Hybrid approaches in turn leveraged complementary information, improving predictive performance and reducing the sensitivity of environmental suitability estimates to sampling biases. Main conclusions Ultimately, we show how the synergistic integration of experimental ecology with observational biogeography can lead to more accurate and ecologically robust predictions for species distributions and their environmental responses to climatic changes.

papers.title: Quantifying floral rewards: Comparative evaluation of nectar extraction techniques
papers.abstract: 1.) Nectar is a crucial resource for a wide range of insect species and one of the driving forces shaping plant-pollinator interactions. Flowers have evolved diverse strategies to restrict nectar access, ensuring only beneficial flower visits resulting in successful pollination. This range of adaptations, often morphological, makes it difficult for researchers to collect nectar in a standardised manner. In this study, we compare common methods used for nectar extraction, with a focus on applicability across several plant families 2.) We assessed pre-treatment methods widely used before nectar extraction, such as pollinator exclusion by bagging flowers, storing flowers overnight in water, and standing nectar crop (unmanipulated control). Moreover, we compared the effectiveness of two commonly used nectar extraction techniques, i.e., centrifugation and microcapillaries, across a range of flower morphologies. We compared nectar volume, sugar concentration, and total sugar content obtained by different methods for 23 flower species from 16 plant families. 3) We show that pollinator exclusion by bagging is an effective measure to obtain maximum nectar volume regardless of plant growth type. The nectar sugar concentration of herbaceous and woody species showed pre-treatment specific variation. Extraction with a centrifuge consistently yielded more nectar volume without altering the sugar concentration, while microcapillary extraction was not effective for most flower morphologies, especially lip (e.g. Salvia pratensis) and disc-shaped flowers (e.g. Rosa canina). 4.) Our results provide a foundation for the standardisation of floral nectar extraction protocols, improving comparability across studies, and facilitating broader ecological and evolutionary research that depends on consistent and reliable nectar sampling.

papers.title: Validating regional insect pest phenology forecasts using published developmental data
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Crop losses caused by insect pests are expected to increase under global warming, highlighting the need for accurate phenology forecasts to support integrated pest management (IPM). Arthropod pests, as ectotherms, exhibit temperature-dependent development and phenology that can be described by thermal performance curves (TPCs). For decades, developmental models have predicted pest emergence through thermal accumulation approaches, yet it remains unclear to what extent experimentally derived development models can accurately predict field phenology across spatial and temporal scales. Here, we evaluate whether developmental TPCs and linear degree-day models fitted from published experimental data can predict large-scale pest phenology under a rate-summation approach. RESULTS: We compiled published developmental data for the widespread crucifer pest Pieris rapae and fitted several TPCs and linear degree-day models. Model predictions were validated against independent long-term monitoring data from the Catalan Butterfly Monitoring Scheme for mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands. Published experimental data accurately predicted large-scale pest emergence, with prediction errors generally below one week. However, predictive performance depended strongly on the spatial and temporal scale considered, with model rankings changing according to the scale and temperature resolution used. CONCLUSION: Published experimental thermal biology data can accurately predict regional insect pest phenology when developmental models are selected according to the intended forecasting scale. These findings provide practical guidance for improving pest alert systems and other decision-support tools, while demonstrating how decades of experimental research can be translated into operational phenology forecasting.

papers.title: Evaluating the effectiveness of raised beds in alleviating heavy metal contaminants
papers.abstract: Structural policy and social practices, including redlining and white flight, have driven disinvestment and heightened exposure to persistent environmental pollutants resulting from residual impacts of industrial activity. Urban agriculture, meant to empower and feed communities, are frequently established on vacant lots that may contain these contaminants and pose a threat to human health. To circumvent the legacy of contaminations on bare soil, Chicago growers are using raised beds to create a barrier between contaminated soil and healthier imported compost. Our goal was to assess the efficacy of this barrier system by 1) quantifying eight heavy metals and Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs) between existing soils and raised beds, 2) examining the difference between key soil properties, and 3) determining the environmental risk determined by their potential ecological risk index (PERI). We expected that metal concentrations would vary across sites and soil types, and raised beds would have fewer heavy metals than existing soils. Our results showed existing soils generally had higher levels of heavy metals with significant differences in lead and arsenic, suggesting that raised beds could be a viable barrier system. We also found higher levels of phosphorus, nitrogen, and magnesium in raised beds than existing soils. Thirdly, lead and copper significantly increased with pH while arsenic and copper decreased with organic matter levels. Despite the presence of heavy metals, the sites had a lower risk of environmental contamination, indicating that growers' extra measures to ensure their soils are safe to grow food may be sufficient, barring metal- and site-specific strategies.

papers.title: Freezing seawater samples alters the community composition and richness inferred from eDNA metabarcoding
papers.abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has become a common approach for surveying biodiversity, yet processing aquatic samples can sometimes be challenging in the field. When eDNA water sample processing is delayed during remote field collections, whole water samples can be stored frozen to minimize further eDNA degradation. However, the freezing and thawing processes may influence eDNA integrity thus affecting species identification. We split bulk seawater samples to compare the marine taxa detected from water that had been filtered immediately to water that had been stored frozen for one month. Using DNA metabarcoding targeting a 313bp section of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) mitochondrial barcode gene, we evaluated the effect of freezing on the inferred marine invertebrate communities. We found that previously frozen samples had significantly lower species richness and different community composition compared to the non-frozen samples. Particularly, amplified sequence variants (ASVs) of the copepod Pseudocalanus were significantly more abundant in non-frozen samples. These data suggest that freezing water samples intended for eDNA analyses may impede species detection for select organisms and significantly alter the inferred community structure. Studies using pre-frozen water samples should consider downstream implications when analyzing eDNA biodiversity.

papers.title: Modeling Coupled Ecohydrological and Structural Responses to Forest Thinning
papers.abstract: Forest thinning is a silvicultural practice widely used to reduce competition among trees and enhance forest resilience. However, its long-term coupled effects on forest water balance and canopy structure remain uncertain due to competing hydrological processes, disturbances, and climatic variability. This study developed a multiyear stochastic ecohydrological model coupling soil saturation and water fluxes with canopy structure, represented by dynamic leaf area index (LAI), to examine how thinning alters soil water storage and evapotranspiration (ET) as the canopy regrows. Simulations were conducted for historically thinned forest sites, parameterized using FLUXNET climate data and species/stand-level traits obtained from the TRY database and published literature, with thinning intensity represented by initial LAI reductions ranging from 0% to 50%. Results show that long-term soil saturation responses and canopy recovery rates vary substantially across sites, while total ET remains relatively stable following thinning, as increased soil evaporation and greater water availability for the remaining canopy can compensate for reductions in stand-level transpiration. These findings highlight the importance of site-specific conditions in determining forest ecohydrological responses and the potential water conservation benefits of thinning.

papers.title: Environmental and particle trait controls on microbial carbon turnover on fast-sinking particles in the Iceland Basin
papers.abstract: Microbial remineralisation of sinking particles governs the depth and magnitude of organic carbon sequestration in the ocean. Yet, the combined influence of environmental gradients and particle morphology in regulating remineralisation remains poorly constrained. During spring in the subpolar Icelandic Basin, we estimated microbial carbon turnover, a proxy for remineralization, on fast sinking particles collected at two depths below the mixed-layer using shipboard incubations. Alongside this we used imagery to determine the morphology and complexity of the particles. Microbial carbon turnover exhibited strong depth-dependent variability, with generally higher rates in shallower samples and substantial variability among stations and sampling days. Fast-sinking particle assemblages were dominated by aggregates and detrital material, while faecal pellets comprised only a minor fraction of particles, and particle diversity decreased with depth. Environmental variables, particularly chlorophyll-a concentration, explained over 80% of observed variability in microbial carbon turnover. Particle traits describing size, size heterogeneity and structural complexity were also significant predictors, increasing model explanatory power to 91%. Larger and more heterogeneous particle assemblages were associated with lower microbial carbon turnover, while increased structural complexity was associated with lower turnover after accounting for particle size. Together these findings indicate that particle traits provide additional controls on microbial carbon turnover beyond environmental variables alone.

papers.title: Cross-level correlation and temporal dynamics of hierarchical habitat selection
papers.abstract: Habitat selection is a fundamentally hierarchical process implying that choices made by animals at broad spatial scales constrain those made at finer ones. How selection for the same habitats relates across hierarchical orders remains largely untested empirically. We investigated whether selection for a given habitat at the larger scale reinforces itself, is independent of, or opposes selection for the same habitat at the finer scale. Using GPS-collared European hares (Lepus europaeus, n = 52) in a mid-mountain grassland landscape (French Jura, 2021-2023), we jointly quantified and compared temporal variation in second-order (home range placement within the landscape) and third-order (habitat use within home ranges) selection with generalised linear mixed models, and resource selection functions. The association in selection strength between orders was strongly habitat-dependent: significantly positive for grasslands, forests and farm tracks, but negative for fodder crops. Our results suggest that hierarchical levels of habitat selection can couple or decouple depending on the habitat considered and what resources European hares are seeking at the different scales. Temporal variability in selection was consistently greater within home ranges than at the landscape level, and seasonal variation in ecological conditions (temperature, precipitation) shaped fine-scale selection while leaving landscape-level selection largely unaffected. Large-scale selection by European hare appeared relatively stable over time while fine-scale selection allowed dynamic behavioural adjustments to short-term variability of environmental conditions. Our results illustrate a hierarchical strategy of stable placement of the home range, flexible use within it. Reliance on heterogeneous open and semi-open habitats and consistent avoidance of built-up areas also clarifies the habitat requirements of the European hare in grassland-dominated agricultural landscapes, given population declines across much of its native range.

papers.title: Taxonomic turnover with phylogenetic conservation in subaerial biofilm (SAB) communities of marble monuments
papers.abstract: Subaerial biofilms (SABs) colonizing exposed stone surfaces provide natural systems for investigating microbial community assembly under challenging environmental conditions. Although bacterial diversity on stone has been widely described, whether taxonomic variation reflects broader phylogenetic and ecological differences remains unclear. Here, we characterized SAB communities inhabiting two geographically separated historic urban marble monuments, Federal Hall National Memorial (New York) and the Lincoln Memorial (Washington, DC), using SSU rRNA amplicon sequencing. Additional samples from the Merchants' Exchange Building (Philadelphia) were also examined. Bacterial communities exhibited pronounced taxonomic turnover but substantially greater phylogenetic similarity, indicating that community variation primarily reflected replacement among closely related bacterial lineages rather than turnover among distantly related clades. Despite this taxonomic turnover, core assemblage analyses identified conserved bacterial lineages shared across monuments, several of which were also detected in the independent Philadelphia samples. Consistent with these patterns, inferred ecological composition remained remarkably similar among monuments, with chlorophyll-containing bacteria dominating all communities. Together, these findings demonstrate that these monuments harbor distinct bacterial assemblages while maintaining a conserved phylogenetic and inferred ecological framework, suggesting that environmental filtering and local ecological processes may contribute to SAB community assembly across spatial scales.

papers.title: Ecology of Chagas disease vector Triatoma sanguisuga in Delaware: distribution, habitat, host use and Trypanosoma cruzi infection
papers.abstract: Chagas disease is a vector-borne disease caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi and transmitted by triatomine bugs. The disease is increasingly recognized as an emerging public health threat in the United States (US). Little is known about the Chagas disease system in the Mid-Atlantic US despite the presence of a native T. cruzi vector species, Triatoma sanguisuga. The species is widespread throughout the eastern US, and the Mid-Atlantic comprises the northernmost portion of its geographic range. Triatoma sanguisuga has been implicated in autochthonous T. cruzi transmission to humans in other parts of the US but has never been formally studied in the Mid-Atlantic. To fill this knowledge gap and increase public health preparedness, we investigated T. sanguisuga in Delaware and eastern Maryland. We aimed to collect baseline information about the species, including its habitat, feeding patterns, and T. cruzi infection rates across land use intensities. We collected 151 T. sanguisuga specimens in all three DE counties and two counties in MD, and identified standing dead trees as an important local habitat for the species. Twenty specimens (13.2%) were submitted by community members who had found the bugs in or around human homes and businesses. We detected T. cruzi infection in 23 of 150 (15.3%) specimens and identified 24 vertebrate host species, including humans, from 95 specimens. We detected a stage-structured blood feeding pattern wherein juvenile bugs ("nymphs") were reptile-associated (which are refractory T. cruzi hosts)and adult bugs were mammal-associated (which are competent T. cruzi hosts), which was reflected in a significant difference in T. cruzi infection prevalence between adults and nymphs. Our findings reveal the multiscale network that sustains T. cruzi transmission in Delaware while also providing practical public health information on a local vector-borne disease system.

papers.title: Identifying key biodiversity areas in Mozambique for conservation planning and policy
papers.abstract: The world is experiencing unprecedented rates of biodiversity loss. To reverse this trend, signatories to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) have committed to conserving at least 30% of marine and terrestrial areas by 2030, with an emphasis on sites critical for biodiversity. One mechanism to support this goal is the identification of Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) to inform spatial planning and the development of conservation area networks. However, few case studies demonstrate how the KBA process can be implemented in high-biodiversity, low-income countries. We present a national-scale example from Mozambique, where KBAs were delineated across seven taxonomic groups, and outline a post hoc theory of change to support broader national implementation and progress towards CBD targets. We describe how the project established institutional arrangements and training to build technical capacity, highlighting the central role of the Ministry of Land and Environment. We then present the KBA identification process and results, including species Red List assessments that contributed to the identification of four marine and 25 terrestrial KBAs. With results integrated into national policy and legislation, the Mozambique KBA system demonstrates that KBA identification is feasible in lower-income countries and provides a model for broader application.

papers.title: Physiological diversity and the assembly of nitrifying communities in aerobic granular sludge
papers.abstract: One-stage partial nitritation/anammox systems provide a cost-effective and efficient approach to nitrogen removal, but its wide application for sewage treatment remains a challenge. Four key ecological dynamics determine its success: i) the protection of anammox bacteria from oxygen exposure by nitrifiers, ii) the inhibition of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria through residual ammonia accumulation, iii) the competition for oxygen among nitrifiers, and iv) the competition for nitrite between nitrite-oxidizing bacteria and anammox bacteria. Using a comprehensive Individual-based Model, we simulate the ecological interactions among microbial communities under relevant operational and environmental conditions, emphasizing the role of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria diversity by differentiating Nitrobacter, Nitrospira and Nitrotoga genera. Our simulation experiments identify and quantify the fundamental constraints when optimizing one-stage partial nitritation/anammox systems, particularly the challenge of suppressing nitrite-oxidizing bacteria while maintaining a strong anammox activity. Notably, our results show that the previously observed stratification between ammonia- and nitrite-oxidizing communities, does not indicate optimal nitrogen process partitioning. These findings highlight the limitations of relying solely on operational design to control community structure, as this approach may fail to ensure stable and efficient nitrogen removal across diverse conditions in one-stage partial nitritation/anammox systems.

papers.title: Global biodiversity indicators do not fully capture how land cover alters species richness and composition
papers.abstract: Global biodiversity indicators of land-use impact are increasingly used to track international targets and to inform corporate disclosure, yet few have been tested against independent field data. Because species richness and community composition can change independently, an indicator capturing only one can miss changes in the other. Using standardized bird surveys on three continents, I show that most of seven leading indicators ranked sites within ecoregions no better than the share of natural land cover, for both richness and composition. I developed new estimates of how land cover affects richness and composition, from GBIF occurrence records open to commercial use, and tested them in the same surveys. Only the new composition estimate clearly outperformed natural-cover share for composition, and the new richness estimate predicted field richness as well as an expert-range map in two of three regions. Neither estimate could stand in for the other. Globally, assessments depended on the natural reference: cropland retained about half of the bird species of a forest reference but four-fifths of those of an open natural one. Assessing the state of nature therefore requires an explicitly justified reference, and indicators that report richness and composition as a pair and are tested against independent surveys.

papers.title: Global indicators of climate-driven shifts in vertebrate assemblages
papers.abstract: We develop global indicators for tracking how species assemblages respond to climate change by estimating community climate indices based on species maximum temperature and minimum aridity niche limits. We applied them to global databases using 33.6 million occurrence records from the past half-century to track assemblage changes for 26,163 species of terrestrial vertebrates. Changes in community climate indices tracked climate changes, weakening at higher elevations and strengthening at higher latitudes. Species that disappeared from sampled locations were intolerant of hot and dry conditions, while colonising species were characteristic of warmer and drier locales. Trends differed markedly within subcontinental regions, ecoregions and countries. Many vertebrate assemblages are responding to climate change yet lags in some regions and countries raise concerns that they are not keeping pace.

papers.title: Transit mortality and the efficiency of Tamarixia radiata releases against Diaphorina citri in metapopulation networks
papers.abstract: Augmentative releases of the parasitoid Tamarixia radiata are a main tool against Diaphorina citri, the vector of huanglongbing in citrus, but release models usually treat orchards as a single patch. We extended a four-compartment model of psyllid, flush, parasitoid and plant vigour with impulsive releases to networks of eight patches coupled by diffusion of psyllids and parasitoids, with optional transit mortality, and compared uniform releases with releases targeted at the outbreak patch. Without transit mortality the amount released dominated the outcome. Uniform releases reduced the network pest load by about 30% and targeted releases by 2.5-4.5%, efficiencies per parasitoid were similar, and topology changed the pest load by less than 2%, mainly through the degree of the outbreak patch. The master stability function ranked the networks by spatial coherence but did not account for its level over an outbreak. Parasitoid transit mortality created an intermediate dispersal rate that maximised the efficiency of targeted releases without minimising the pest load. This optimum lay where transit losses pushed the resident parasitoid towards collapse, so that the pest load without releases rose sharply. A linear invasion argument explains why it scales with the mean degree and the mean edge mortality.

papers.title: Cold acclimation and diapause independently improve egg cold tolerance and act through distinct mechanisms in the invasive mosquito Aedes albopictus
papers.abstract: 1. Phenotypic plasticity is an important mechanism by which organisms can cope with environmental change. However, there is growing recognition that phenotypic plasticity is not a single phenomenon but instead encompasses a range of responses that vary in reversibility and are predicted to evolve under different conditions. Nevertheless, few studies have disentangled the fitness effects and mechanisms of different forms of plasticity, making it difficult to predict their respective roles in promoting population persistence in the face of climate change. 2. In our study, we assessed plasticity of egg cold tolerance in the vector mosquito Aedes albopictus, considering both irreversible plasticity caused by photoperiodically-mediated diapause and reversible plasticity caused by cold acclimation. We also analyzed metabolites and lipids to investigate the extent to which these two forms of plasticity improve cold tolerance through shared mechanisms. 3. We found that diapause and cold acclimation independently enhance cold tolerance of Ae. albopictus eggs. While the beneficial effect of diapause on cold tolerance persisted throughout our experiment, cold tolerance gained through acclimation was lost when eggs were returned to warm temperatures. 4. Cold tolerance plasticity in Ae. albopictus does not appear to be driven by the accumulation of classical cryoprotectants. Instead, reductions in citric acid cycle intermediates and free fatty acids imply that diapause induces metabolic suppression, which likely helps maintain energy balance during winter and may also improve cold tolerance by protecting against cold-induced disruption of metabolic homeostasis. Cold acclimation generally increased lipid unsaturation, which may function to preserve membrane fluidity at low temperatures. Overall, diapause and cold acclimation imparted largely nonoverlapping effects on egg metabolite and lipid profiles, indicating that these two forms of plasticity act through distinct molecular pathways. 5. In addition to identifying potential mechanisms by which an invasive vector mosquito attains cold tolerance to survive winter, our results provide evidence that irreversible and reversible plasticity are distinct phenomena capable of evolving independently during populations' responses to novel environmental conditions.

papers.title: Parental effects can be transmitted through the rhizosphere microbiome
papers.abstract: Plant responses to environmental changes, including to competition by neighboring plants, can be influenced by soil microbes. They can also be modified through parental effects, which can transmit environmental cues across generations and shape plant phenotypes through various mechanisms such as epigenetic modifications. However, we do not yet know whether parental effects in plants can also act through modifications of the rhizosphere microbiota. Here, we grew eight genotypes of Phragmites australis with or without interspecific competition, and examined its transgenerational effects on offspring phenotype and rhizosphere microbial communities in a common environment. We found that competition decreased plant growth in a genotype-specific manner, but plants whose parents had been exposed to competition previously shifted their functional phenotypes towards a more conservative resource strategy. Notably, parental competition also altered the diversity and community structure of rhizosphere soil bacteria and fungi in offspring plants, and structural equation models indicated that these soil microbiome changes may have driven some of the observed changes in offspring phenotypes. Our study demonstrates that parental environmental effects can influence offspring traits not only directly, but also through alteration of rhizosphere microorganisms, and that parental effects are more complex than we previously knew.

papers.title: Thermal Similarity Attenuates the Strength of Bergmanns Rule in Birds
papers.abstract: Geographic body size variation, classically framed as Bergmann's rule, is a fundamental indicator of temperature-mediated morphological adaptation. However, empirical support for Bergmann's rule in birds remains highly unpredictable across lineages. We hypothesized that this variation is caused by differences in thermal similarity among species within the same genus, which may limit temperature driven changes in body size and be influenced by ecological factors. Using a global dataset comprising 5,715 bird species across 513 genera, we observed that thermal similarity was the strongest predictor of variation in the strength of Bergmann's rule among competing hypotheses. Among genera exhibiting significantly negative body mass temperature relationships, higher thermal similarity was consistently associated with less negative slopes, indicating weaker Bergmannian clines. Subgroup analyses indicated that the positive thermal similarity slope association was supported in dense and semi open habitats and among nonmigratory birds, but was not clearly supported in open habitats or among migratory birds. Our findings provide a novel explanation for variation in the strength of Bergmannian clines among avian lineages, showing that stronger morphological differentiation along thermal gradients is associated with greater thermal contrast. Consequently, our findings provide a basis for testing whether incorporating thermal similarity and ecological context can improve forecasts of avian morphological responses to ongoing climate change.

papers.title: hilldiv3: a unified Hill-number framework for neutral, phylogenetic and functional diversity analysis in R
papers.abstract: 1. Hill numbers provide a coherent family of diversity measures that can incorporate phylogenetic relatedness and functional trait dissimilarity, but applying them consistently across neutral, phylogenetic and functional diversity, and across measurement, partitioning and (dis)similarity, still requires combining several packages with incompatible conventions. 2. We present hilldiv3, an R package that provides per-sample diversity, nested multiplicative partitioning across scales for all three diversity types, bounded (dis)similarities and pairwise matrices, diversity profiles, evenness and redundancy, and the allocation of Hill power sums and dissimilarities to taxa or taxonomic sets. 3. hilldiv3 directly supported all twelve benchmarked combinations of operation and diversity type, and built pairwise (dis)similarity matrices 15-820 times faster than hilldiv2 and hillR, with up to two orders of magnitude less memory. We showcased the package by analysing Microflora Danica data (360 samples, 5,518 genomes, eight habitats), demonstrating that neutral, phylogenetic and functional diversity turned over at very different rates between habitats, and a near-constant Actinomycetota share concealed opposing shifts of two orders. 4. By deriving every metric from the same Hill-number formulation, hilldiv3 makes neutral, phylogenetic and functional results directly comparable, and lowers the barrier to rigorous diversity analysis of community-ecology and high-throughput sequencing data.

papers.title: Pervasive ethanol in the fruits and floral nectars consumed by tropical frugivores
papers.abstract: Dietary ethanol has long been proposed as a selective force shaping the diets and physiology of tropical frugivores and nectarivores, yet this idea has rested on measurements from only a few species and sites. Here, we present the first global survey of ethanol in wild fruits and flowers (591 and 37 species, respectively, across 18 countries) and test ecological and phylogenetic predictors of its variation. We detected ethanol in the ripened fruits of 72% of angiosperm species (211 species, N [≥] 3 per species; 0.021% - 3.9% alcohol by volume (ABV)). Ethanol was also detected in the flowers of 12 species (0.037% - 0.73% ABV). Maximum fruit ethanol varied with temperature, humidity, and phylogenetic relatedness, and it was higher in ripe fruits collected from the forest floor relative to their canopy counterparts. We then extrapolated potential daily ethanol consumption for 10 primate species. Estimated maximum daily ethanol ingestion for primates ranged from negligible to 0.72 g/kg/day on average (equivalent to 5.1 international standard drinks, 10 g ethanol each, for a 70 kg human). Our findings show that ethanol is widespread in plant reproductive tissues and shaped by both phylogeny and environment, supporting the hypothesis that dietary ethanol has been a pervasive selective pressure on fruit- and nectar-feeding animals.

papers.title: Formalizing host competence
papers.abstract: Host competence, the capacity to acquire, sustain and transmit parasites or pathogens, is typically quantified for species, although it is also an individual property. We derive an individual-level competence index from infection biology and link it to reproduction numbers. Our index separates infectiousness and susceptibility (individual properties) from contact and abundance (environmental properties); combined, they yield host potential and capacity, analogues of vector potential and vectorial capacity. We simulated populations in four systems (Lyme disease, West Nile virus, chytridiomycosis, avian influenza), using experimental data where available and plausible values otherwise. Individual competence varied widely within and overlapped among species; species means approximated an established index for West Nile virus, to which the model was calibrated. Under the assigned variances, intraspecific variation was greatest in low-competence species, whose loads sit near the transmission threshold; there, load-contact covariation roughly halved or doubled mean potential. Where contact was measured (Lyme tick burdens), nearly all individuals of high-competence species replaced themselves across plausible tick survival, whereas replacement by most individuals of low-competence species depended on tick survival. In West Nile virus, the most infectious 20% of mourning doves supplied about half of transmission, so species averages could understate the role of some individuals.

papers.title: Rapid estimation of insect biodiversity using AI assisted image analysis:a cost-effective tool for monitoring and ecological assessmen
papers.abstract: Protection of natural areas and environmentally friendly management of anthropogenic landscapes require reliable tools for monitoring and comparing biodiversity. Bioindicator-based approaches can support large-scale ecological assessment, but insect monitoring remains constrained by the taxonomic expertise required for species identification. Here, we propose an AI-supported index for estimating the biodiversity of flying insects, based on the diversity of visual features of insect bodies. Flying insects were captured using yellow sticky traps across agricultural and natural habitats, seasons, crops, and sites in Israel's Mediterranean region. Traps were scanned at high resolution and uploaded to a dedicated image database. A machine learning model was used to detect and delineate insects, after which engineered visual features representing body size, color, and shape were extracted. Biodiversity was estimated from distances among feature vectors and compared with taxonomic diversity derived from expert identification of a representative validation set. The AI-derived diversity index correlated strongly with expert-based taxonomic diversity, supporting the hypothesis that morphological variation in insect images can provide a proxy for taxonomic diversity. Applying the index to the full dataset revealed a negative relationship between insect abundance and diversity, while diversity also varied across habitats and sampling seasons. Our results demonstrate the potential of AI-based image analysis to provide rapid and cost-effective assessments of insect biodiversity without requiring complete taxonomic identification. This approach may facilitate biodiversity monitoring and support timely ecological assessment and decision-making in sustainable agricultural and landscape management.
